Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Rabbi
  trauma_type: Refugee
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared, Visual (Weapons): Weapons or objects used as weapons, Shouting: Shouting
  Maladaptive Strategies: Punishment Thinking: I tell myself I deserve to suffer because of what happened, Distraction: I distract myself with something else, Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Safe Seat Seeking: I always choose where to sit based on how safe or protected I feel, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
  Negative Appraisals: Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Others-Would-Cope: Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

Vignette:
Elias remembered the border crossing in the deep winter, thirty-five years ago. The cold had seeped into his bones, but it was the suddenness that lodged in him. A soldier’s rifle barrel had flashed in the dim light, catching his eye, while a sharp shout tore through the gathered crowd. When a stranger’s hand clamped onto his arm without warning, pulling him forward, Elias had flinched so violently he nearly fell. He had come to believe that someone in charge, someone with more authority, should have stopped it before it unfolded. His PCL5 score of 57 confirmed what he had felt in his body: a steady, moderate load of symptoms that did not chase each other, but simply occupied the same space. In the years that followed, his body began to act as if the border crossing were still unfolding. A quick tap on his shoulder from a congregant made his heart hammer against his ribs, and he would catch himself thinking that his own physiology was betraying him. He could not rely on his own reactions to signal safety; a steady pulse felt like a deception. In his synagogue, a place of study and sanctuary, he learned to navigate the physical space with quiet calculation. He always chose where he would sit based on how protected he felt from behind and to the sides, preferring the third pew near the pillar where he could watch the doors and rest his back against solid wood. Over time, he only felt truly safe within a narrow circle of rooms: his study, his bedroom, and the synagogue’s lower office. When he stepped outside that perimeter, he often distracted himself with the text of the Torah, tracing the letters until the world narrowed to the page. Yet, even in the synagogue, triggers found him. A raised voice during a service made him glance toward the source, certain the shout from the border was echoing back. He watched objects with the same wariness as he watched people; a heavy brass menorah, a letter opener on his desk, a guest’s coat hanger swung too quickly—all carried the potential of a weapon. He avoided emotional closeness with his partner, standing as a separate habit alongside his physical wariness. Intimacy required him to let his guard down in spaces that felt suddenly vulnerable, and he let that distance settle. He told himself he deserved to carry this weight, as if surviving had been a kind of passing the buck, and his quiet endurance was the penalty he owed for what had happened. As a rabbi, his daily work demanded a steadiness that his body often refused. During evening prayers, he would struggle to concentrate on the readings, his attention snagging on the unexpected brush of a visitor’s sleeve or the sharp cadence of a congregant’s voice. He had come to believe that the body’s constant vigilance was not a sign of weakness but a warning he could not ignore. His seat selection had become nonnegotiable; the sanctuary’s center rows felt exposed, while the aisle seats near the exit offered a clear path. His symptoms did not drive one another; they simply accumulated. His body kept its own schedule, his avoidance of closeness ran parallel to his seat preferences, and his punishment thinking coexisted with his daily distraction. Now at sixty-three, Elias found himself seeking help not because the world had grown more dangerous, but because the steady exhaustion of constant monitoring had made him wonder if he had been carrying a false ledger. He wanted to understand why his body still braced for impact when his hands were empty, and he hoped to stop telling himself he deserved the strain. What frightened him most was not the trigger itself, but the unsteady ground beneath his own judgment, and what he hoped for was a way to sit in the third pew near the pillar without feeling that the shout was only seconds away.
